title: The Universe at Large
body:
ASTR 1103 covers everything beyond the solar system: how stars work, how they end, how galaxies
are built out of them, and how the universe as a whole has changed. It is a descriptive course,
so the mathematics stays at the level of proportions and the emphasis is on the chain of
reasoning behind each claim.

That chain is the point. Nobody has visited a star, so every number in the course was inferred
from light arriving at a telescope. The course is organised around what can be extracted from
that light: its brightness gives distance once the true output is known, its colour gives
temperature, its [[Spectra|spectrum]] gives composition, and its shift gives motion. Each
technique is built on the one before it, which is why the sequence matters more here than the
individual facts.

The physics is [[CLASSICAL PHYSICS 1]] applied at a scale where the numbers stop
being intuitive. Orbital motion is [[Uniform Circular Motion]] with gravity supplying
the centre-seeking force, and a star holds its shape by a force balance that is a
[[Free-Body Diagram]] written for a sphere of gas.

## Topics

### Distance, and the size of everything

The first problem is units, because the numbers are otherwise unreadable.
[[Astronomical Distance]] defines the three that get used. An astronomical unit is the
Earth-Sun distance, about 150 million km, and suits the solar system. A light-year is how far
light travels in a year, about $9.5 \times 10^{12}$ km, and suits nearby stars. A parsec is
3.26 light-years and comes from the parallax measurement below.

The light-year also carries a fact worth holding on to: looking further away means looking
further back in time, so every observation in the course is a historical record.

[[Stellar Parallax]] is how the first rung of the distance ladder is measured. A nearby
star appears to shift against the distant background as Earth moves across its orbit, and the
distance follows from the size of that shift:

```
d (parsecs) = 1 / p (arcseconds)

Proxima Centauri:  p = 0.768"   ->   d = 1.30 pc = 4.25 light-years
```

The shift is tiny and shrinks with distance, so parallax runs out after a few thousand parsecs
and the later methods in the course exist to take over from it.

### What light carries

[[Spectra]] is the technique the rest of the course depends on. Spreading light by wavelength
produces one of three patterns, and each says something different:

```
continuous   a smooth rainbow            a hot dense object, such as a stellar interior
emission     bright lines on dark        a hot thin gas, emitting at its own wavelengths
absorption   dark lines on a rainbow     a cool gas in front of a hot source
```

The lines sit at wavelengths fixed by the element producing them, so a spectrum identifies
composition from any distance. A star shows an absorption spectrum, because its cooler outer
layers absorb from the continuous spectrum generated below.

[[Blackbody Radiation]] connects colour to temperature. Wien's law puts the peak
wavelength at $\lambda_{max} = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}/T$, so a 5800 K star peaks at 500 nm in the
visible and a 3000 K star peaks in the infrared and looks red. The Stefan-Boltzmann law makes
the energy output go as $T^4$, so doubling a star's temperature multiplies its output per unit
area by
16. Between them, a star's colour gives its temperature and its temperature plus its size give
its total output.

[[Doppler Effect]] gives motion along the line of sight. Spectral lines shift toward red
when the source recedes and toward blue when it approaches, and the size of the shift gives the
speed. Since the rest wavelengths are known exactly, the measurement is precise, and it is what
supplies stellar masses in a binary system, galactic rotation curves, and the expansion of the
universe.

### Measuring a star

Two brightnesses have to be kept apart. Apparent brightness is how bright a star looks from
here, and luminosity is how much energy it actually emits. They differ because of distance,
through the [[Inverse-Square Law]]: light spreads over a sphere whose area grows as $d^2$,
so a star twice as far away appears a quarter as bright.

That relationship is used in both directions. Knowing distance and apparent brightness gives
luminosity. Knowing luminosity and apparent brightness gives distance, which is what a standard
candle is, and it is how the distance ladder continues past parallax.

The [[HR Diagram]] is the organising plot of stellar astronomy, with temperature on one
axis and luminosity on the other. Stars fall into a few regions and leave most of the plot
empty, and the regions turn out to be stages of a life cycle. About 90% sit on the main
sequence, a diagonal band, and a star's position along it is set almost entirely by its mass.
The mass-luminosity relation makes luminosity rise steeply with mass, so a star ten times the
Sun's mass is thousands of times brighter and exhausts its fuel far sooner.

[[Binary Stars]] are where mass is measured directly. Two stars orbiting a shared centre
obey Kepler's laws, so the orbital period and separation give the total mass, and the ratio of
the two orbits gives the individual masses. Almost every stellar mass in the course traces back
to a binary measurement.

### How a star lives

[[Star Formation]] begins with a cold cloud in the interstellar medium collapsing under
its own gravity. Conservation of angular momentum makes the collapsing cloud spin faster and
flatten into a disc, which is why planetary systems are flat. Compression heats the core, and
when it reaches roughly 10 million K, fusion starts.

[[Main Sequence]] is the long stable stage that follows, and stability comes from a
balance: gravity pulling inward against pressure from the fusing core pushing outward. That
balance is self-correcting, since a core that contracts gets hotter and fuses faster, which
pushes back out. A star sits on the main sequence for as long as its hydrogen lasts, which is
about 10 billion years for the Sun and a few million for the most massive stars.

The [[Solar Neutrino Problem]] is the worked example of how the course's claims get
tested. Fusion predicts a specific flux of neutrinos from the Sun's core, and detectors
measured about a third of it for thirty years. The resolution changed particle physics and left
the solar model intact, since neutrinos oscillate between types in flight and the early
detectors saw only one type.

### How a star ends

The ending is decided by mass, and the course follows two paths.

A low-mass star exhausts its core hydrogen, contracts, and starts fusing in a shell around the
core, which expands and cools the outer layers into a [[Red Giant]]. The outer layers
drift off as a planetary nebula and the exposed core remains as a [[White Dwarf]], held up
by electron degeneracy pressure with no fusion inside it. That support fails above the
Chandrasekhar limit of about 1.4 solar masses, which is why every white dwarf is below it.

A high-mass star fuses heavier elements in shells until it reaches iron, which absorbs energy
to fuse where every earlier stage released it. The core collapses in seconds and rebounds,
producing a [[Supernova]] bright enough to outshine its galaxy. Everything heavier than iron in
the universe, including the iron in blood, was made in that event or in a similar one.

What remains depends on the core mass. Below about 3 solar masses it becomes a
[[Neutron Star]], a city-sized object with the density of an atomic nucleus, observed as a
pulsar when its beam sweeps past Earth. Above that limit no known pressure resists gravity and
the collapse continues to a [[Black Hole]], whose event horizon sits at the Schwarzschild
radius, $R = 2GM/c^2$, which is 3 km for the Sun's mass and 9 mm for Earth's.

### Galaxies

The [[Milky Way]] is a barred spiral about 100,000 light-years across, with the Sun
roughly 27,000 light-years from the centre. Its structure was worked out from the inside, which
is the difficulty: mapping a galaxy you are sitting in means inferring the shape from
directions and distances, since no vantage point outside it exists.

Its rotation curve is the surprise. Orbital speed should fall with distance from the centre
once most of the mass is inside the orbit, in the way planets orbit slower further from the
Sun. Measured speeds stay flat far past the visible edge, which means far more mass is present
than is emitting light. That is the evidence for [[Dark Matter]], and it is confirmed
independently by the motion of galaxies within clusters and by gravitational lensing.

[[Galaxy Classification]] sorts galaxies into spiral, elliptical and irregular, with the
Hubble tuning fork as the traditional arrangement. [[Active Galactic Nuclei]] covers
the small fraction whose centres outshine everything else in them, powered by matter falling
onto a supermassive black hole, with quasars as the most extreme and most distant examples.

### Cosmology

[[Hubble's Law]] states that a galaxy's recession speed is proportional to its distance,
$v = H_0 d$. Every distant galaxy is receding, and the further one is, the faster it goes,
which is what expanding space produces. Nothing is at the centre of the expansion, because
every observer sees the same pattern.

Running the expansion backwards gives an age. With $H_0 \approx 70$ km/s per megaparsec,
$1/H_0$ is about 14 billion years, which is the [[Big Bang]] timescale derived from one
measurement.

The [[Cosmic Microwave Background]] is the direct evidence. The early universe was
hot, dense and opaque, and it became transparent when it had cooled enough for atoms to form.
The light released at that moment is still arriving, stretched by the expansion into microwaves
at 2.7 K, and its near-uniformity across the sky with tiny fluctuations is what every model of
structure formation has to reproduce.

The fate of the universe depends on its density and the geometry that follows from it, which
the course covers descriptively, along with the observation that the expansion is accelerating.

## Related courses

- [[CLASSICAL PHYSICS 1]] (PHYS 1201) supplies the mechanics. Orbits are
  [[Uniform Circular Motion]] with gravity as the centre-seeking force, hydrostatic balance in
  a star is a [[Free-Body Diagram]], and the collapse of a gas cloud conserves angular
  momentum the way [[Linear Momentum]] is conserved in a collision.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199) explains what a [[Spectra|spectrum]] is
  mathematically, since decomposing light by wavelength is decomposing a signal into
  frequencies, which is the [[Fourier Transform]].
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234) is how a measurement becomes a claim here, since every
  astronomical quantity carries an uncertainty and the [[Solar Neutrino Problem]] was a
  three-decade disagreement between a prediction and a measurement.
- [[CALCULUS 1]] (MATH 1200) supplies the [[Limit]] behind an inverse-square field and the
  integration behind a luminosity summed over a sphere.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] is how modern surveys classify galaxies, since
  [[Galaxy Classification]] by eye stops working at millions of images and becomes a
  [[Classification]] problem for a [[CNN]].
